transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?
I came in because I’ve started doing things that scare me. I’ll walk out in the middle of a deployment, or drive around late at night with no plan. That’s not how I’ve ever handled stress before.
During these times when you walk out or drive off, do you ever lose track of who you are or have trouble remembering what happened afterward?

I don’t lose track of who I am. But parts of what happened are missing. I remember the contractor’s face and the noise really clearly, and then there’s this whole chunk in the middle—I know I was there, but I just can’t bring it back.
Did these episodes start shortly after a specific frightening or traumatic event, and if so, how long ago was that event?
Yes. It started after that late-night cutover incident—it's been a little over a year now, about 13 months.
Since that night, have you been having intrusive memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the incident, or feeling constantly on edge and easily startled?

Yes. It can come out of nowhere—especially if I’m in that conference area, or somebody raises their voice on a call. I get these images and sounds from that night so strongly that I lose track of what I was saying.
During these episodes when you walk out or drive off, do you ever end up somewhere and realize you have no memory of how you got there or why you went there?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed ending up somewhere and having no idea how I got there.

latest_inference.note: Patient denies ending up somewhere with no memory of how/why she got there, ruling out dissociative fugue (F44.1). Symptoms of intrusive memories, flashbacks, hyperarousal, and partial amnesia for the traumatic event, all emerging after a specific trauma 13 months ago, are consistent with PTSD with dissociative features (F43.1).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient developed a cluster of symptoms beginning approximately 13 months after a clearly identifiable traumatic event (a late-night cutover incident with a frightening confrontation). Core PTSD features are present: intrusive, vivid re-experiencing of sensory fragments (the contractor's face, the noise) triggered by reminders (conference room, raised voices), hyperarousal/startle, and impaired concentration during flashbacks. There are also dissociative amnesia gaps for portions of the traumatic memory and impulsive escape behavior (walking out, driving aimlessly at night), which are recognized dissociative/avoidance features that can occur within PTSD, rather than a separate fugue disorder—the patient retains identity and does not describe travel with loss of personal identity or complete amnesia for the fugue episodes themselves (denies waking up somewhere with no memory of how/why), arguing against dissociative fugue (F44.1) as primary diagnosis. The temporal link to trauma, symptom content, and pattern best fit chronic/delayed-onset PTSD with dissociative features.

confirmed_symptoms: Intrusive vivid images/sounds from the traumatic night
Flashback-like intrusions triggered by reminders (conference area, raised voices)
Loses track of what she was saying during triggered episodes
Driving around late at night with no plan
Partial amnesia for portions of the traumatic memory (gap in the middle of the event)
No reported episodes of waking up somewhere with no memory of travel/reason for being there
